# Collection of orthopedic conditions

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General orthopedics > Collection of orthopedic conditions*

[Original Article Link](/library/i50JPg)

---

## Summary

This article covers various orthopedic conditions including <u>myositis ossificans</u>, <u>joint contractures</u>, <u>ganglion cysts</u>, <u>trochanteric bursitis</u>, <u>pes anserine bursitis</u>, meniscal cysts, and <u>heel pad syndrome</u>.

---

## Myositis ossificans

<u>Myositis ossificans</u> (<u>heterotopic ossification</u>) is a benign, <u>heterotopic ossification</u> of <u>soft tissue</u> and/or <u>skeletal muscle</u> that either occurs congenitally or, more commonly, following <u>soft tissue</u> or <u>muscle injury</u>




### Localized course (myositis ossificans localisata)




* Etiology

* Posttraumatic; : especially after implantation of an artificial <u>hip joint</u> or after blunt muscle trauma

* Neurogenic: after nerve injuries, <u>meningitis</u>, and <u>spinal cord injuries</u>

* Chronic degenerative disease (e.g., in <u>ankylosing spondylitis</u>)

* Muscle overuse (e.g., in athletes)

* Clinical features: <u>localized symptoms</u> in the affected muscle/tissue (e.g., <u>quadriceps femoris muscle</u>, <u>brachialis muscle</u>)

* Restriction of movement

* Muscle stiffness

* <u>Pain</u>, swelling

* Palpable <u>soft tissue</u> mass

* Diagnostics

* <u>Soft tissue ossification</u> is detectable on conventional <u>x-ray</u>.

* Radiological findings: <u>periosteal reaction</u> with periarticular <u>soft tissue</u> calcifications (<u>eggshell calcification</u>)

* Laboratory findings: ↑ <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> and <u>ESR</u> levels

* Positive <u>scintigraphy</u>

* <u>Histology</u>: zonal distribution of immature, proliferating <u>fibroblasts</u> that are surrounded by <u>metaplastic</u> <u>trabecular bone</u>

* Differential diagnosis: <u>malignant bone tumors</u> (e.g., <u>sarcoma</u>)

* Treatment: <u>radiotherapy</u>, possibly <u>surgery</u>

* Prophylactic measures against recurrence

* Single dose <u>radiotherapy</u> recommended (possibly postoperative or preoperative)

* Alternative: postoperative administration of <u>NSAID</u> (<u>indomethacin</u>)





### Progressive generalized disease (myositis ossificans progressiva/<u>fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva</u>)




* Etiology: extremely rare, <u>autosomal dominant</u> hereditary disease

* Pathophysiology: <u>Fibrocytes</u> produce <u>bone tissue</u> instead of <u>scar</u> tissue in all types of trauma.

* Clinical features

* Generalized <u>ossification</u> mainly from <u>cranial</u> to <u>caudal</u> (life-threatening if the respiratory muscles are affected)

* <u>Malformation</u> of toes is frequently observed at <u>birth</u>.

* During the course of the disease, large, painful, well-vascularized swellings appear at various sites, which develop into <u>bone tissue</u> after regression.

* Treatment

* No causal treatment

* Symptomatic: <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>radiotherapy</u>, possible surgical removal of individual lesions

## Joint contractures

* Definition: a restriction in <u>joint</u> movement resulting from <u>connective tissue</u> <u>fibrosis</u> in the <u>skin</u>, <u>fascia</u>, muscles, and/or <u>joint capsule</u> adjacent to the affected <u>joint</u>

* Etiology

* Prolonged <u>immobilization</u>, especially bed care patients

* Hospitalization > 2 weeks (especially in the <u>ICU</u>)

* Bed care in the domestic or <u>nursing home</u> setting

* Chronic disease (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, severe burn, <u>stroke</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>)

* Trauma (e.g., <u>fractures</u>, <u>connective tissue</u> injury)

* Congenital disease (e.g., <u>cerebral palsy</u>)

* Clinical features

* Decreased <u>range of motion</u> (<u>ROM</u>) of the affected <u>joint</u>

* <u>Pain</u> when attempting to move or extend the <u>joint</u>

* See also “<u>Dupuytren contracture</u>.”

* Diagnostics

* Assessment of the <u>ROM</u> of the affected <u>joint</u>

* Imaging (to detect <u>connective tissue</u> <u>fibrosis</u>)

* Treatment

* <u>Conservative therapy</u> (e.g., <u>physiotherapy</u>)

* <u>Surgery</u>





References:[[3]](/library/5nciF10)

## Ganglion cyst

* Definition: benign <u>mucin</u>-filled cyst that develops along <u>tendons</u> or <u>joints</u> and has no true <u>epithelial</u> lining

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common type of hand mass

* Location: : wrist and fingers (most common at the <u>dorsal</u> wrist)

* Pathophysiology: <u>herniation</u> of <u>connective tissue</u>;  associated with repetitive trauma and mucoid degeneration of periarticular structures → sac that is lined with synovial cells and contains <u>paucicellular</u> <u>connective tissue</u> (typically <u>mucin</u>)

* Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic but can occasionally cause <u>joint</u> <u>pain</u>

* <u>Fluctuant</u>, transilluminant swelling

* Can lead to nerve compression, which may cause numbness, <u>weakness</u>, or tingling (e.g., <u>Guyon tunnel</u> syndrome)

* Differential diagnoses: <u>epidermoid cysts</u>, <u>lipoma</u>, <u>rheumatoid nodules</u>, <u>infectious tenosynovitis</u>, <u>soft tissue tophus</u>

* Treatment

* Asymptomatic: observation (<u>ganglion cysts</u> often regress spontaneously)

* Symptomatic: <u>aspiration</u> or surgical resection





![Ganglion cyst](media/rx065mhnlpvlzyyh80dlze9a.jpg)

## Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

* Definition: <u>lateral</u> <u>hip pain</u> caused by tendinopathy of the <u>gluteus medius</u> or minimus

* Etiology: : <u>gluteus medius</u> or <u>gluteus minimus muscle</u> tendinopathy

* Involvement of the trochanteric <u>bursa</u> is possible, although rare.

* May also be associated with snapping hip (<u>coxa saltans</u>) or trauma

* Clinical features

* Common cause of <u>lateral</u> <u>hip pain</u>

* <u>Pain</u> is usually localized to the greater trochanter at the <u>proximal</u> end of the <u>femur</u>.

* Tenderness to palpation over the greater trochanter

* <u>Pain</u> is triggered by resisting active <u>abduction</u> or standing only on the affected leg.

* Diagnostics

* Usually, <u>clinical diagnosis</u> is sufficient.

* Imaging may be indicated if the diagnosis is unclear, if underlying pathology is suspected, or in cases that do not respond to initial treatment. [[5]](/library/LWYwNL)

* <u>X-ray</u>: used to rule out other causes of <u>hip pain</u> (e.g., <u>osteoarthritis</u>, <u>femoral neck fracture</u>)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: may show thickening of the <u>iliotibial band</u>, <u>tendinosis</u> of the <u>gluteal muscles</u>, and/or <u>trochanteric bursitis</u> [[6]](/library/oWY0mL)

* <u>MRI</u>: to evaluate for an underlying pathology or prior to <u>surgery</u>

* Treatment [[5]](/library/LWYwNL)

* Mainly conservative

* <u>Physical therapy</u> and <u>relative rest</u>

* Oral <u>NSAIDs</u> or <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections for <u>pain</u>/discomfort

* Management of comorbidities, including <u>back pain</u>, <u>obesity</u>, and <u>leg length discrepancy</u>

* In refractory cases;  (without improvement after > 12 months of <u>conservative management</u>), <u>surgery</u> is indicated (e.g., bursectomy). [[7]](/library/kSXm-x)

## Pes anserinus pain syndrome

* Definition: a condition characterized by <u>pain</u> and tenderness at the anteromedial aspect of the knee

* Components: each of these can be present to varying degrees depending on the patient

* Tendinopathy of the <u>pes anserinus</u>

* <u>Pes anserine bursitis</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Female sex

* <u>Type 2 diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Osteoarthritis of the knee</u>

* Knee <u>arthritis</u>, knee deformities (e.g., knee valgus; , knee varus)

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> on the <u>medial</u> aspect of the knee when rising from a seated position, ascending or descending stairs, and/or sitting with legs crossed

* Worsening of <u>pain</u> at night

* Tenderness over the upper <u>medial</u> <u>tibia</u>   [[8]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Diagnostics

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* <u>Physical examination</u>: assessment of knee alignment, <u>pes anserinus</u> insertion site, <u>pain</u> or tenderness during knee <u>flexion</u> and extension

* No <u>pain</u> on passive <u>external rotation</u> or valgus <u>stress</u>

* Usually no <u>joint</u> instability or swelling

* Imaging

* AP <u>x-ray</u> of the knee: rule out underlying <u>osteoarthritis</u> and <u>stress fractures</u>

* Knee <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u>: indicated in patients with local inflammation and/or induration to rule out other diagnoses (e.g., tumors, <u>meniscal tears</u>, <u>osteonecrosis</u>) that cannot be diagnosed on <u>x-ray</u>

* Differential diagnosis

* <u>Tibial stress fracture</u>

* <u>Medial meniscus</u> injury

* Treatment

* Rest (e.g., avoidance of high or heavy-impact activities), application of ice to the knee

* <u>NSAIDs</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u>: <u>quadriceps</u>-strengthening exercises

* Weight loss in patients with <u>obesity</u>

* Soft <u>knee brace</u>

* <u>Steroid</u> injections: indicated in patients with refractory symptoms, severe <u>pain</u>, or nocturnal <u>pain</u>





![Ligaments and retinacula of the patella](media/xrpl3zbxow3ncjq45v36r0tg.jpg)

## Meniscal cyst

* Definition: a collection of <u>synovial fluid</u> in or around the <u>meniscus</u>

* Etiology: secondary to a <u>meniscal tear</u>  → <u>synovial fluid</u> becomes encysted

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> and swelling

* Decreased <u>range of motion</u> of the knee

* Chronic <u>meniscal tears</u> → locking (decreased extension of the knee) and popping (<u>knee joint</u> laxity)

* Diagnostics

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* <u>MRI</u> can aid in management if surgical intervention is indicated.

* Treatment [[9]](/library/Mu0M73)

* <u>Conservative management</u> with rest, <u>pain control</u>, and crutches

* Surgical intervention is indicated in refractory cases that do not respond to <u>conservative management</u>, or if there are mechanical symptoms (locking, popping) or tears in an avascular zone.

## Heel pad syndrome

* Definition: a condition characterized by damage to the fatty and fibrous tissue in the heel

* Etiology: typically caused by inflammation but can also be due to damage or <u>atrophy</u> of the heel pad

* Acute trauma

* Repetitive overload (e.g., running, prolonged standing or walking)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Age (usually > 40 years old)

* <u>Corticosteroid</u> injections

* Improper footwear

* Cavus feet

* <u>BMI</u> > 30

* Clinical features

* Deep, mid-heel <u>pain</u> that increases with activity and when walking on hard surfaces

* Tenderness in the mid-portion of the heel

* Diagnostics

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* Imaging (<u>x-ray</u>, <u>ultrasound</u>) may be indicated if the diagnosis is unclear.

* Differential diagnosis

* <u>Plantar fasciitis</u>

* <u>Calcaneal stress fracture</u>

* Treatment: mainly conservative

* Rest (decrease/avoid pressure to the affected area)

* Ice packs

* Oral <u>NSAIDs</u> for <u>pain</u>

* Heel taping

* Heel pads or cups

* Use of proper footwear
